blocks.text: GPU Utilization and Model Overhead
In Part 2, we explored memory-related challenges like fragmentation and duplicate computation.
At this point, it feels like we’ve handled most of the system issues. But two things still feel off:

The GPU still doesn’t seem fully utilized
KV cache is still surprisingly large
Let’s walk through both of these the same way—as they naturally come up when trying to understand the system.
Low GPU Utilization
We know that token generation is sequential. Each token depends on the previous one.
That raises an obvious thought:
If one request is small, why not run many of them in parallel?
Why not just batch requests?
Let’s say a GPU can handle 100 units of work.
One request only uses 5 units.
So naturally, we think:
Why not run 20 requests together and fully utilize the GPU?
This is exactly what batching tries to do.
Where batching starts to break
Batching works well when all requests are similar.
But in real systems:

Requests arrive at different times
Requests have different lengths
Some finish early, others run longer
Example:
Step 1: User A, User B, User C start together
Step 2: User A finishes early User B and C are still running
Now the batch is no longer full.
The GPU starts becoming underutilized again.
Another issue with batching
Traditional batching often waits for a batch to fill before starting.
This introduces latency:

New requests have to wait
GPU sits idle during that wait
Continuous Batching
This leads to a better idea.
Instead of fixed batches, we allow requests to come and go continuously.
How it works
At any point in time:

Running requests continue
Finished requests are removed
New requests are added immediately
Example:
Step 1: User A, User B running
Step 2: User A finishes User C joins immediately
Step 3: User B finishes User D joins
Why this works better

No waiting for batch formation
No wasted GPU slots
Work is always flowing
Intuition
Batching is like waiting for a bus to fill up before leaving.
Continuous batching is like a metro system:

People get on and off continuously
The system never stops
Large Model Overhead
Even after solving scheduling and memory layout, KV cache still feels large.
This leads to a deeper question:
Where is this extra memory coming from?
Understanding attention heads and layers
We already know:
For each token and each layer, we store key and value vectors.
But there’s more structure inside a layer.
Each layer has multiple attention heads.
What does that mean?
Instead of storing one key/value pair per token, we store one per head.
Example:
If a model has 32 heads:
Head 1 → Key₁, Value₁ Head 2 → Key₂, Value₂ ... Head 32 → Key₃₂, Value₃₂
So for one token, we are storing 32 versions of key/value.
Why do we need multiple heads?
Each head captures a different type of relationship in the data.
You can think of it as:

One head focusing on syntax
Another on relationships
Another on context
They provide diversity in how the model understands the sequence.
The problem
This diversity comes at a cost.
Memory now scales with:

number of tokens
number of layers
number of heads
So larger models (with more heads) create much larger KV caches.
MQA (Multi-Query Attention)
This leads to a natural question:
Do we really need separate key/value for every head?
MQA says: not necessarily.
What MQA does

Keep multiple query heads
Share a single key and value across all heads
Before
After
Q1...Q32 K (shared) V (shared)
Why wasn’t this done originally?
Because separate key/value per head gives more flexibility.
Each head can focus on different aspects independently.
Trade-off
MQA reduces memory significantly, but:

Heads lose some independence
Model expressiveness can slightly reduce
Intuition
Originally:
Each head had its own notebook
With MQA:
All heads share one notebook
GQA (Grouped Query Attention)
MQA works well, but sometimes it is too aggressive.
So the next idea is to find a middle ground.
What GQA does
Instead of sharing across all heads, we share within groups.
Example
32 heads grouped into 4 per group:
Trade-off

Better memory efficiency than standard attention
Better quality than MQA
Intuition

Standard: everyone has their own notebook
MQA: everyone shares one notebook
GQA: small groups share notebooks
Putting It All Together
At this point, the system-level picture is clearer:

Continuous batching improves how we use compute
MQA and GQA reduce how much memory the model needs
What Comes Next
So far, we have focused on single-node inference optimization.
The next natural question is:
What happens when a single GPU is not enough?
In the next part, we’ll look at scaling inference across multiple GPUs and systems.
